findings.explanation: The /dev/sdb block_device_mapping sets volume_type = "standard" (magnetic), a previous-generation EBS type with unpredictable, low IOPS (best-effort, ~40-200 IOPS) and no burst/baseline performance guarantee. gp3 offers a 3,000 IOPS / 125 MB/s baseline at a flat, predictable price with no per-request I/O charges, and is the current AWS-recommended default for general-purpose volumes.
findings.remediation: Change volume_type to "gp3" for the /dev/sdb mapping (and consider adding explicit iops/throughput if the bastion workload needs more than baseline).
findings.title: Launch template uses legacy magnetic (standard) EBS volume for secondary disk

findings.explanation: var.common_tags was only wired into aws_security_group.instance_ssh_access (aws_security_group.instance_ssh_access.tf:25). The ASG had no `tag` blocks. Note: provider-level default_tags (set by callers, e.g. example/examplea/provider.aws.tf) does NOT cover aws_autoscaling_group, since it uses a custom `tag` block implementation rather than a plain `tags` map -- so this couldn't be solved at the provider level and needed a module-level fix.
findings.remediation: Propagate tags to the ASG via a dynamic `tag` block with propagate_at_launch = true, so launched instances inherit them.
findings.resolution_note: var.common_tags was removed from the module entirely (module now relies on caller-configured provider default_tags). Since default_tags does not propagate to aws_autoscaling_group's custom tag block, the gap is bridged with a data "aws_default_tags" lookup merged with var.name for the instance Name tag.
findings.title: var.common_tags is declared but never applied to the compute resources it names

findings.explanation: most_recent = true combined with a wildcarded name filter ("amzn2-ami-hvm-*-x86_64-ebs") means the resolved image_id can change on any future `terraform plan/apply` whenever Amazon publishes a new AMI in that family -- with no code change and no review. Because the launch template has create_before_destroy = true, this can trigger an unreviewed, unplanned instance replacement of the bastion.
findings.remediation: Pin the AMI: expose it as an input variable with a default AMI ID, or pin via an SSM parameter data source read at a known version, so the image only changes on an explicit, reviewable update.
findings.title: AMI lookup is unpinned (most_recent + wildcard name filter), so repeated applies can silently select a different image

findings.explanation: Unlike example/examplea/terraform.tf, the root module ships no terraform{} block at all, so there is no required_version and no required_providers constraint on the aws provider it depends on. Consumers can pull this module in with an incompatible Terraform or AWS provider version with no upfront error -- failures surface late, as plan/apply errors instead.
findings.remediation: Add a terraform.tf with a required_providers block constraining the aws provider (e.g. version = ">= 6.0, < 7.0") and a required_version for Terraform itself, mirroring example/examplea/terraform.tf.
findings.title: Root module has no terraform{} / required_providers block

suggested_policies.rationale: aws_launch_template / aws_launch_configuration block_device_mappings using volume_type = "standard" is unambiguous and always a downgrade versus gp3 -- there is no scenario where magnetic is the right default for a new template. This fires deterministically on any Terraform declaring the attribute.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_AWS_262
name: Launch template EBS volumes should not use legacy magnetic (standard) type
principle: cost
severity: LOW
rationale: |
  volume_type = "standard" is the previous-generation magnetic EBS type with
  best-effort, unpredictable IOPS and per-I/O pricing. gp3 provides a flat-rate
  baseline of 3,000 IOPS / 125 MB/s at a comparable or lower price and is the
  AWS-recommended default for general-purpose workloads.
remediation: |
  Set volume_type = "gp3" (or "gp2"/"io1"/"io2" if higher performance is
  required) instead of "standard".
resources:
  aws_launch_template:
    path: block_device_mappings.ebs.volume_type
    not_equals: standard

suggested_policies.rationale: data.aws_ami with most_recent = true and a wildcarded name filter is a well-known repeatability trap: the resolved AMI silently changes between applies whenever a new image is published upstream. This is a structural pattern (specific data source + specific attribute combination) that fires deterministically regardless of the surrounding module.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_TF_077
name: aws_ami data source should not combine most_recent with a wildcarded name filter
principle: repeatability
severity: LOW
rationale: |
  most_recent = true paired with a filter.name value containing "*" means the
  resolved AMI can change on any future plan/apply with no code change, causing
  unplanned instance replacement in downstream resources that reference
  image_id. Pinning to an explicit AMI ID or a versioned SSM parameter makes
  image updates an explicit, reviewable action instead of implicit drift.
remediation: |
  Pin the AMI explicitly: expose the AMI ID as an input variable with a
  reviewed default, or resolve it via an SSM parameter data source pinned to a
  known parameter version, rather than resolving most_recent against a
  wildcarded name pattern.
resources:
  data.aws_ami:
    path: most_recent
    equals: false
